title: Mori–Nagata: normalization of a Noetherian domain is Krull
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian integral domain [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], where integral domain means $1\ne0$ and $xy=0$ implies $x=0$ or $y=0$. Let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ be its field of fractions $a/b$ with $a,b\in R$ and $b\ne0$, and let $N\subseteq K$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $K$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. Then $N$ is a Krull domain. A commutative integral domain $A$ is called Krull if (i) for every height-one prime $P$ (a nonzero prime with no prime strictly between $(0)$ and $P$), $A_P$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is a Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] normal domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]; (ii) $A=\bigcap_{\mathrm{ht}(P)=1} A_P$ inside $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$; and (iii) every nonzero element of $A$ belongs to only finitely many height-one primes. An empty intersection inside a fraction field means that whole field.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 (Mori–Nagata), printed pp. 90–91, specialized to a domain (one minimal prime); Definition 4.10.1, printed p. 89. Author-hosted PDF read online at https://www.math.purdue.edu/~iswanso/book/SwansonHuneke.pdf; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: First $\operatorname{Frac}(N)=K$: both inclusions follow from $R\subseteq N\subseteq K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$. For a height-one prime $Q\subset N$, [lem-trf-normalization-finite-local-model] gives a Noetherian local domain $C_p\subset K$ of dimension one whose integral closure in $K$ is $N_Q$. Its fraction field is $K$, because $R\subseteq C_p\subseteq K$. Apply [lem-sc-krull-akizuki-noetherian] with base $C_p$, extension $K/K$ of degree one, and intermediate ring $N_Q$; this proves $N_Q$ Noetherian. Apply [lem-sbc-integral-closure-finite-normal-product] to $R\to K$, viewing the field $K$ as the single normal factor. It gives normality of every $N_Q$. This proves clause (i).

source.place: Lemma 4.9.4 and Theorem 4.10.5, first domain paragraph, printed pp. 88, 90; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: For $0\ne x\in N$, write $x=a/d$ with $0\ne a,d\in R$. If a height-one prime $Q$ contains $x$, then $a=dx\in Q\cap R$. By [lem-trf-normalization-height-one-associated-contraction], $Q\cap R$ belongs to $\operatorname{Ass}_R(R/aR)$. This is finite by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-associated-primes-finite], since $R/aR$ is generated as an $R$-module by $1$. Over each of these finitely many contractions there are only finitely many primes of $N$, by [lem-trf-normalization-finite-prime-fibres]. Their finite union contains all the height-one primes containing $x$. This proves clause (iii), globally, before proving the intersection assertion.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 proof, printed p. 90, finite-character paragraph; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: For clause (ii) it suffices to prove the assertion when $R$ is local. Indeed, for each maximal ideal $m\subset R$, put $S=R\setminus m$. The ring $R_m$ is Noetherian: every ideal of $R_m$ is the extension of its contraction to $R$, whose finite generators also generate the localized ideal. By [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-commutes-localization], $S^{-1}N$ is its integral closure in $K$. The prime correspondence for localization sends its height-one primes to height-one primes $Q$ of $N$ disjoint from $S$: every prime below $Q$ is also disjoint from $S$, so the strict prime chains below $Q$ are unchanged. The further localizations are $N_Q$, directly from their fractions. Thus an element in all global height-one localizations belongs to every $S^{-1}N$ once the local assertion is proved. The final step below will recover $N$. For Steps 4-15 now assume $R$ local; Steps 1-2 still apply.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 proof, printed pp. 90-91, reduction to the local case; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Use [lem-trf-normalization-completed-product-comparison] for this local $R$. In its notation the complete Noetherian local domains $B_i=\widehat R/q_i$ have fraction fields $L_i$ and normalizations $T_i$, and there are compatible embeddings $j_i:K\hookrightarrow L_i$ with $N=\{x\in K:j_i(x)\in T_i\ \forall i\}$. Each $B_i$ is Nagata by [lem-weil-pbc-complete-local-nagata]. Its prime $(0)$ therefore has Japanese quotient $B_i$; [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain], with the degree-one extension $L_i/L_i$, says that $T_i$ is a finite $B_i$-module. Module generators also generate it as a $B_i$-algebra, since every element is a linear combination of them. Hence [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian] makes $T_i$ Noetherian. This obtains exactly the finiteness input of Theorem 4.3.4 from existing DAG nodes.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 proof, printed p. 91; Proposition 4.7.3; Theorem 4.3.4, finite-normalization consequence (existing Stacks 032W and 032F route); author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sbc-integral-closure-finite-normal-product] to $B_i\to L_i$: every prime localization of $T_i$ is a normal domain. Then [lem-weil-pbc-normal-domain-of-local-normal] gives normality of $T_i$ itself. For $0\ne b\in T_i$ and $a\in T_i$, [lem-weil-pbc-normal-domain-principal-quotient-associated-height] puts every associated prime of $T_i/bT_i$ in height one. If $a/b$ belongs to every height-one localization, then for each such associated prime $Q$ some $s\notin Q$ has $sa\in bT_i$, so the class of $a$ vanishes at $Q$. The injectivity in [lem-weil-pbc-module-injects-localizations-associated-primes] makes that class zero. Thus $T_i=\bigcap_{\operatorname{ht}Q=1}(T_i)_Q$ inside $L_i$. Each $(T_i)_Q$ is Noetherian by the finite-generation argument for localized ideals in Step 3, normal as above, local, and one-dimensional by the prime-chain definition of height; [lem-sc-normal-dim1-dvr] makes it a DVR.

source.place: Proposition 4.10.4 and its use in Theorem 4.10.5, printed pp. 90-91; the intersection proof is also Stacks 031T(1)-(2), via 0311; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: For each pair $(i,Q)$ from Step 5, take the integer-valued valuation $v_{i,Q}:L_i^\times\to\mathbf Z$ of the DVR $(T_i)_Q$, as in [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], and restrict it along $j_i$ to $K^\times$. Write these restricted valuations as $v_\lambda$. Steps 4-5 give $N=\{0\}\cup\{x\in K^\times:v_\lambda(x)\ge0\ \forall\lambda\}$. For each $0\ne a\in N$, only finitely many $\lambda$ have $v_\lambda(a)>0$: there are finitely many factors $i$, and in each $T_i$ a height-one prime containing the nonzero $j_i(a)$ is minimal over $j_i(a)T_i$, since no nonzero prime lies strictly below it. Now apply [lem-sc-finite-minimal-primes-over-ideal] to the Noetherian $T_i$. Discard valuations trivial on $K^\times$, since their inequalities impose no condition. For each remaining valuation its centre $p_\lambda=\{0\}\cup\{a\in N\setminus\{0\}:v_\lambda(a)>0\}$ is a nonzero prime: primality follows by additivity and nonnegativity; to see nonzeroness write an element of positive value in $K=\operatorname{Frac}(N)$ as $c/d$, so $v_\lambda(c)>v_\lambda(d)\ge0$.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 proof, printed p. 91, normalized completed branches; integer valuations are Proposition 4.1.3/Stacks 00PD; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: The representation just obtained localizes as follows. For any multiplicative subset $S\subset N\setminus\{0\}$, keep the indices $\lambda$ for which $v_\lambda(s)=0$ for every $s\in S$. Then $S^{-1}N$ is exactly the intersection of the nonnegative valuation rings for these indices. One inclusion is immediate. For the other, write $x=a/b\in K^\times$ with $a,b\in N\setminus\{0\}$. Only finitely many indices have $v_\lambda(x)<0$, because each has $v_\lambda(b)>0$. None is kept, so choose $s_\lambda\in S$ of positive value for each of these indices, and a positive integer $n_\lambda$ with $n_\lambda v_\lambda(s_\lambda)+v_\lambda(x)\ge0$. For $s=\prod s_\lambda^{n_\lambda}\in S$, every valuation of $sx$ is nonnegative: the other factors all lie in $N$ and cannot lower any value. Thus $sx\in N$ and $x\in S^{-1}N$. Zero is automatic. In particular for $S=N\setminus P$ the kept indices are exactly those with $p_\lambda\subseteq P$.

source.place: Exercise 4.30, printed p. 96; explicit denominator-clearing argument used in Theorem 4.10.5, printed pp. 91-92; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Fix $0\ne b\in N$. Let $F=\{\lambda:v_\lambda(b)>0\}$, which is finite by Step 6. For $\lambda\in F$, put $J_\lambda=\{0\}\cup\{a\in N\setminus\{0\}:v_\lambda(a)\ge v_\lambda(b)\}$. The valuation representation gives $bN=\bigcap_{\lambda\in F}J_\lambda$: if $a$ belongs to the right side, then every valuation of $a/b$ is nonnegative, including the indices outside $F$ where $v_\lambda(b)=0$. Hence $a/b\in N$. The reverse inclusion follows by additivity. If $F$ is empty this says $bN=N$.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 proof, printed p. 91, finite primary decomposition of bN from the completed branches; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Each $J_\lambda$ is an ideal by the valuation inequalities, has radical $p_\lambda$, and is $p_\lambda$-primary: if $ac\in J_\lambda$ with $a\notin p_\lambda$, then $v_\lambda(a)=0$ and $c\in J_\lambda$. A positive-valued element has a power of value at least $v_\lambda(b)$, proving the radical assertion. Moreover $p_\lambda^{e_\lambda}\subseteq J_\lambda$ for $e_\lambda=v_\lambda(b)\ge1$, since a product of $e_\lambda$ positive integer values has sum at least $e_\lambda$, and sums preserve the lower bound. Merge the finitely many ideals with the same radical, then delete redundant terms. Intersections of primary ideals with the same radical are primary by the displayed test, and taking the maximum of their power bounds retains a power bound. We obtain an irredundant expression $bN=J_1\cap\cdots\cap J_t$ with distinct prime radicals $p_j$ and $p_j^{e_j}\subseteq J_j$; every $p_j$ is the centre of at least one retained valuation.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 proof, printed pp. 91-92; explicit primary and prime-power calculations in the DVRs; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: The smaller principal-height subclaim [lem-trf-normalization-principal-height-one-refinement] applies to the present local Noetherian base $R$ and its normalization $N$. Thus every prime $P$ containing a nonzero $c\in N$ contains a height-one prime containing $c$. We use only this refinement, not any finiteness or height-one intersection assertion from that node. The remaining steps prove that the primary radicals of Step 9 must have height one.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 proof, printed p. 91, paragraph beginning We next prove that for any non-zero element b; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Suppose, to get a contradiction, that one radical $p_1$ in Step 9 is not height one. It is nonzero since it contains $b$. There must be a retained index $\mu$ with $p_\mu\subseteq p_1$ and $v_\mu(b)=0$. Otherwise Step 7, for the multiplicative subset generated by $N\setminus p_1$ and $b$, gives $N_{p_1}[1/b]=K$ (no index remains). Every nonzero prime of $N_{p_1}$ would then contain $b$: for $0\ne h$ in it, write $h^{-1}=a/b^n$ in $N_{p_1}[1/b]$, so $b^n=ha$ belongs to it. In particular all height-one primes below $p_1$ contain $b$, and there are finitely many by Step 2 and the prime-chain correspondence of Step 3.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 proof, printed pp. 91-92, finite prime-avoidance argument (A.1.1) written out; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Choose the least positive integer $h$ for which $p_1^h\cap J_2\cap\cdots\cap J_t\subseteq bN$. It exists by the prime-power bound for $J_1$. There is $c\in p_1^{h-1}\cap J_2\cap\cdots\cap J_t$ outside $bN$: for $h>1$ this is minimality, and for $h=1$ it is irredundancy of the decomposition (with $p_1^0=N$). Then $cp_1\subseteq bN$, since multiplication puts the result in $p_1^h$ while preserving all other $J_j$. In particular $c\ne0$. Put $z=c/b\in K\setminus N$.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 proof, printed p. 92, minimal prime-power exponent and the choice of c; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: For $d\in P$, one has $zd\in N$ by $cP\subseteq cp_1\subseteq bN$. If $d\ne0$, then $v_\mu(zd)=v_\mu(c)+v_\mu(d)-v_\mu(b)>0$, since $c\in N$ and $v_\mu(b)=0$. Thus $zP\subseteq P$. Choose $0\ne d\in P$, possible because trivial restricted valuations were discarded in Step 6. Inductively $z^nd\in P\subseteq N$ for every $n\ge1$. For every index $\lambda$, $nv_\lambda(z)+v_\lambda(d)\ge0$ for all $n$; the values are integers, so $v_\lambda(z)\ge0$. The representation of Step 6 forces $z\in N$, contradicting Step 13. Therefore every radical $p_j$ in Step 9 has height one.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 proof, printed p. 92, valuation argument excluding embedded primary components; zero-centre valuations explicitly removed; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Distinct $p_j$ are now incomparable. Localizing $bN=\bigcap_jJ_j$ at $p_i$ kills every $J_j$ with $j\ne i$: choose $s\in p_j\setminus p_i$ and a power of $s$ in $J_j$. Hence $bN_{p_i}=(J_i)_{p_i}$. Also $J_i=N\cap(J_i)_{p_i}$, since $sa\in J_i$ with $s\notin p_i$ implies $a\in J_i$ by primarity. Finite intersections localize by multiplying the finitely many witnessing denominators. If $x=a/b\in K$ belongs to every height-one localization of $N$, then $a\in bN_{p_i}$ and therefore $a\in J_i$ for every $i$. Thus $a\in bN$ and $x\in N$. This proves clause (ii) for local $R$. Empty decompositions give $bN=N$, so the same reasoning covers units and fields.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.5 proof, printed p. 92, final paragraph; author-hosted text read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Return to arbitrary $R$ as in Step 3. Let $x\in K$ belong to all height-one localizations $N_Q$. For every maximal ideal $m\subset R$, the local case just proved applied to $R_m$ gives $x\in (R\setminus m)^{-1}N$. The ideal $I=\{r\in R:rx\in N\}$ therefore contains an element outside every maximal ideal. It cannot be proper, since every proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal; hence $1\in I$ and $x\in N$. The reverse inclusion into every $N_Q$ is immediate. Together with Steps 1-2 this proves all three Krull clauses. If there are no height-one primes, the intersection is $K$ and this argument shows $N=K$, agreeing with the stated empty-intersection convention.
